I won’t produce a caption for the image. Instead, based on the aggregate metrics and the image-grounded critiques, here are concise, actionable changes to the global captioning prompt to improve CLIP image–text alignment (focus on adding discriminative, verifiable visual detail and avoiding vague language).

Recommended prompt additions and edits (add as explicit rules in the global prompt):

1. Favor literal, verifiable detail; avoid metaphors, emotive language, guesses about relationships or intent (e.g., don’t assume “friends” or “chasing” unless clearly shown).

2. Always state exact counts for visible people/animals/major objects and their arrangement (e.g., “three people in a horizontal line, left-to-right”). Replace group labels with counts unless a role is visually obvious.

3. Describe precise actions and the physical parts involved (use specific verbs): e.g., “pushing the bicycle by the handlebars,” “riding with rear wheel lifted,” “jumping with both feet off ground.” If a part is interacting (front/rear wheel, right hand), name it.

4. Report colors, materials, and distinctive object details for salient items: clothing colors and styles, accessories (hats, bags), bike/frame/rim color, brick vs. stone facades, roof color, visible tattoos, etc.

5. Anchor scene with concrete background landmarks and setting elements: trees, embankment, crosswalk, fences, tent drapes, arches, water, Ferris-wheel–like structures. Use positional language (foreground/midground/background; left/center/right).

6. Specify camera viewpoint and shot type when visible: high-angle / low-angle / overhead / close-up / wide shot; mention if viewpoint looks down, up, or level with subjects.

7. Describe lighting and shadow cues: backlit/rim light, long shadows, hard sunlight, high contrast, spotlight, overcast. State direction of major cast shadows when visible.

8. Mention notable small objects and their relative positions (e.g., “yellow ball mid-air above center,” “red bag on handlebars, right side”). Indicate if objects are airborne and where relative to people.

9. Describe ground and surface texture when informative (e.g., cracked salt flat, dirt track, paved crosswalk) and any empty or open horizon lines.

10. Prefer concrete architectural details over region labels: number of stories, window shape/arrangement, façade material, roof type/color, visible ornamentation.

11. Avoid vague quantifiers and generics: replace “several,” “some,” “a group,” “wheels airborne,” “a European city,” with specific counts, parts, and descriptors.

12. Keep captions concise but information-dense: one sentence is fine—prioritize discriminative nouns/adjectives (objects, colors, counts, positions, actions, viewpoint, lighting). Do not pad with stylistic flourishes.

13. Add an explicit rule: only assert what is visually present; do not infer unseen relationships or motivations.

How to integrate into prompt text (short template lines to insert):
- “Include: exact counts + left/center/right arrangement; precise action verbs and which body/vehicle part is involved; object colors/materials; one-line camera viewpoint; one-line lighting/shadow cue; one-line background landmark. Avoid speculation and metaphors.”

These changes force captions to include discriminative, verifiable tokens (counts, colors, parts, positions, textures, viewpoint, lighting, unique landmarks) that improve CLIP alignment while reducing generic or speculative phrasing.

new_prompt:
Produce exactly one concise, information‑dense caption (one grammatical sentence) describing only visibly present facts. Output exactly one sentence and nothing else.

Follow this ordered checklist and include each item only if clearly visible; omit unverifiable items. Use digits for counts. Do not infer, hedge, or use metaphors (no "appears/likely/seems"). Keep the sentence compact (prefer ≤30 words) and comma‑separate short phrases.

Order and rules:
1) Start with numeral(s) (digit) + subject noun(s) + precise spatial anchor for each counted subject (left/center/right and foreground/midground/background). If subject is partly out of frame, state "partially cropped at [edge]".
2) Immediately after, include a single visible action if present, and specify the body/vehicle part or object involved (e.g., "right hand on handlebar", "left foot stepping", "rear wheel off ground"). If no clear action is visible, use the token "no-action-visible" or omit the action.
3) Add 1–3 high‑signal descriptor(s) (prefer material/texture, readable text, reflection/wetness, or a distinctive accessory). If legible text appears, transcribe it exactly and localize it (e.g., "'NO PARKING' stenciled on roll-up door at background right"). Cap descriptors to 1–3 short facts (color + material/unique accessory preferred).
4) Choose exactly one viewpoint token if discernible: close-up | medium | wide | high-angle | low-angle.
5) Choose exactly one lighting token if visible: backlit | front-lit | rim-lit | long-shadow-left | long-shadow-right.
6) Choose exactly one short background landmark/texture phrase if visible (single noun phrase, e.g., "wet pavement with ripples", "yellow picnic table", "roll-up door", "plywood roof").
7) For people interacting with structures, require pose + placement wording (e.g., "clinging to top edge near peak, legs dangling"). For visible building construction, include clear cues when present (exposed studs, plywood, insulation).
8) No hedging, no inferred attributes (age, emotion, relationships) beyond visible appearance (hair color, clothing, accessories). Use compact, active phrasing and concrete nouns.

Ordering to follow in the sentence: numeral(s) + subject(s)/location, action+part (if any), discriminative descriptor(s) (max 3), viewpoint token, lighting token, background token.

Examples:
Positive (desired): "3 children center foreground, right child stepping in ankle‑deep puddle; blue raincoat with yellow drawstrings and sunglasses on center child's forehead; medium; backlit; beige van behind."
Negative (avoid): "Several kids standing in water, some wearing colorful clothes, a vague busy background with unclear objects and lighting."

textgrad_loss_text:
Summary recommendation: tighten the checklist into a prioritized, actionable prompt that forces precise, verifiable, and discriminative visual facts (actions, body parts, accessories, materials/textures, signage/text, spatial anchors and framing), limits filler, and gives short token examples for viewpoint/lighting/background so the model produces shorter, higher-CLIP captions that match visible cues.

Concrete, reusable prompt changes

1. Prioritize discriminative facts first
   - Require the caption to first name count + subject(s) + a single, specific visible action (prefer concrete verbs tied to body/vehicle parts, e.g., "right hand on handlebar," "left foot stepping") before other descriptors. This pushes the model to state what distinguishes the image.

2. Force limb/part/object interaction language
   - Explicitly instruct: if an action is shown, describe which body/vehicle part is involved (e.g., "holding by the handlebars," "leaning with forearm on fountain edge," "rear wheel raised"); if not visible, omit. This reduces vague verbs ("standing," "climbing") and increases alignment with visual features.

3. Require material/texture and wetness/reflectivity when visible
   - Ask for concrete surface/material cues (metal/plastic/wood/brick, perforated/reflective/wet/puddled with ripples) and visible wetness/reflective effects (reflections, splashes, droplets). These words are high-signal for CLIP.

4. Require transcription/localization of visible text and markings
   - Explicitly tell the model to transcribe any legible text and localize it (e.g., "yellow 'NO PARKING' stenciled on roll-up door at background right") when clearly readable. Visible text is a strong discriminative feature.

5. Require concrete spatial framing and crop status
   - Add explicit instruction to state subject location (left/center/right and foreground/midground/background) and whether subjects are partially cropped/out of frame. Anchor background objects by position relative to subjects (e.g., "beige van behind center child, wheel visible").

6. Encourage concise, specific clothing/accessory descriptors
   - Ask the model to prefer a few highly distinctive apparel/accessory attributes (color + unique detail: "blue raincoat with yellow drawstrings and red belt," "sunglasses perched on forehead") instead of many generic adjectives.

7. Enforce short standardized viewpoint/lighting/background tokens
   - Provide a small canonical vocabulary and require exactly one token each (examples): viewpoint = {close-up, wide shot, high-angle, low-angle}; lighting = {backlit, front-lit, long shadow left/right}; background = single landmark/texture phrase (e.g., "roll-up door," "yellow picnic table," "wet pavement with ripples"). This reduces verbosity and keeps the model focused on image-level cues.

8. Require visible pose details for dynamic scenes and construction/structure detail for architecture
   - For people on structures, require pose + placement (e.g., "clinging to top edge of plywood panel near roof peak, legs dangling") and for buildings ask for visible construction cues (exposed studs, plywood, trusses, insulation) when evident.

9. Make omission explicit and penalize hedging
   - Reinforce: omit any item that cannot be visually verified; disallow qualifiers like "appears," "maybe," "seems," "likely." This maintains factuality and prevents weak, generic captions.

10. Limit length and ordering
    - Instruct: produce exactly one grammatical sentence, follow the ordering: numeral(s) + subject(s)/location + action+part + discriminative descriptors (clothing/accessory/material/texture/text) + viewpoint token + lighting token + background token. Keep total length constrained—prefer <= 20–30 words of dense facts.

11. Add explicit examples (1–2) in the prompt
    - Give one positive example that shows the target compact style and one negative example that demonstrates overlong/vague output. Concrete examples help the model internalize desired density and wording.

These revisions will push captions toward high-information, visually grounded strings (precise actions, body/part interactions, materials/textures, signage and spatial anchors) that CLIP favors, while reducing vague filler that dilutes similarity.

textgrad_loss_text:
Summary guidance to revise the global captioning prompt (concise, actionable changes to increase image-text discriminativeness and CLIP alignment):

1. Require explicit, anchored counts and spatial anchors for every clearly visible subject (digit + noun + left/center/right + foreground/midground/background). Rationale: CLIP benefits from exact object tokens and locations.

2. Replace vague “no-action-visible” defaults with mandatory micro-action checks: first look for any limb/object contact, gaze, posture, or interaction (e.g., “right hand on fretboard,” “leaning over fountain ledge”); use "no-action-visible" only when absolutely no motion/contact is observable. Rationale: actions strongly disambiguate scenes for CLIP.

3. Mandate description of visible object parts and object–body relations when present (e.g., “left hand on fretboard,” “rear wheel off ground,” “sitting on metal chair beside small round table”). Rationale: part-level cues improve semantic specificity.

4. Prioritize and constrain discriminative descriptors to 1–3 high-signal facts (material/texture, readable text, reflection/wetness, distinctive accessory, color + material). Explicitly rank prefer: legible text > reflection/wetness > material/texture > accessory > color. Rationale: these features boost CLIP similarity more than vague adjectives.

5. Require transcription + localization of any legible text/signage (exact string and location: e.g., "'NO PARKING' stenciled on roll-up door at background right"). Rationale: exact text tokens are high-value for CLIP.

6. Insist on naming salient scene landmarks and surface conditions (water/wet pavement with reflections, stone embankment, storefront window, pier/platform) as a single short noun phrase. Rationale: background landmarks provide strong context signals.

7. Force counting and spatial relations for multiple similar objects (boats, people, bags) and describe relative positions (center, left, right, flanking). Rationale: numeric + positional tokens reduce ambiguity.

8. Require precise clothing/grooming and small-prop details when clearly visible (e.g., “gray blazer,” “polished shoes,” “cap,” “takeaway cup”) but cap to 1–3 descriptors to keep captions compact. Rationale: these are discriminative and visible cues for CLIP.

9. Enforce one explicit viewpoint token and one explicit lighting token only when visually determinable (close-up|medium|wide|high-angle|low-angle; backlit|front-lit|rim-lit|long-shadow-left|long-shadow-right). If not clearly visible, omit. Rationale: avoid adding noisy tokens that hurt matching.

10. For scenes with structures/objects being used (market stalls, boats, storefronts), require a short pose+placement phrase describing how people interact with the structure (e.g., “crouching at display, holding knife”). Rationale: interaction context is highly salient.

11. Prohibit inference, hedging, and metaphors; enforce concrete nouns and visible facts only. Add an explicit "no inference" check-step in the prompt. Rationale: avoids hallucinated tokens that reduce CLIP alignment.

12. Limit sentence length (suggest ≤30 words) and require comma-separated short phrases in a single grammatical sentence; preserve the strict field ordering. Rationale: compact, ordered phrasing yields denser, higher‑precision embeddings.

13. Add a short inference checklist in the prompt that the model must run before emitting caption: (1) verify any action/contact, (2) check for legible text, (3) inspect background for landmarks/reflections, (4) scan for small props/clothing details. Rationale: systematic checks reduce missed discriminative cues seen in low-performing examples.

14. Provide a handful of positive/negative micro-examples in the prompt that demonstrate adding small, visible details (text, reflections, instrument parts, props) versus bad generic outputs. Rationale: few-shot exemplars help the generator apply the rules.

Applying these changes will push captions toward denser, verifiable visual tokens (counts, locations, actions, materials, text, reflections, props) that CLIP heavily weights, and reduce omissions/hallucinations that currently lower image-text similarity.

Summary goal: tighten and reweight the prompt’s visual‑cue requirements so captions name the actual visible objects, small discriminative props, and part‑level interactions (not dataset priors or vague verbs), and to enforce the existing descriptor priority and ordering.

Concrete prompt edits (reusable, global):

1) Enforce strict visual naming: require concrete object nouns visible in the image (e.g., "pier/pavilion", "hard hat", "acoustic guitar", "goal net"), not generic substitutes. If multiple similar objects exist, count them with digits and give spatial anchors (left/center/right + foreground/midground/background).

2) Make the micro‑action checklist mandatory: before emitting, verify limb/object contact, gaze, posture, object displacement, or interactions; if any present, include a part‑level action phrase (body part or object part + verb + target), otherwise use "no-action-visible" only when absolutely none detected.

3) Require small discriminative objects and their relative positions: include visible props (ball, instrument case, pennant, tip box) and state their location relative to the subject (e.g., "ball to right", "case on ground"). These often carry high CLIP signal.

4) Prioritize and cap descriptors exactly as intended: allow up to 3 descriptors per the priority order A>reflection/wetness>B>material/texture>C>accessory>D>color>E; explicitly prefer legible text transcription first (with quotes and localization) and do not substitute or paraphrase it.

5) Force part‑level relation phrases whenever interaction exists: require one concise relation phrase for physical interactions (e.g., "sitting on metal chair", "holding pennant over awning", "rear wheel off ground") to capture contextual relations that improve image-text matching.

6) Require background landmark/texture inclusion if visible: include a single concise background noun phrase (e.g., "stone embankment", "storefront window", "tree‑lined background") to anchor scene context.

7) Insist on directional motion/orientation specificity: when motion is visible, prefer tokens like "mid‑air dive to right", "leaning forward", "standing on fire‑escape platform" rather than vague verbs like "playing" or "running".

8) Transcribe legible text exactly and localize it: if any readable text exists, include the exact string in quotes and its position ("'NO PARKING' on door at background right"); treat this as highest‑priority descriptor.

9) Enforce partial‑frame reporting: if a subject is partly out of frame, require "partially cropped at [edge]" for the relevant subject phrase.

10) Tighten brevity and ordering constraints in the prompt: explicitly instruct models to follow the required ordering and descriptor caps, and to aim for ≤30 words—this reduces filler and forces inclusion of high‑signal items.

11) Add negative examples and corrective rewrites to the prompt: show a few paired examples where a vague caption is rewritten to the required precise form (e.g., "boat"→"pier with small pavilion, 2 boats left/right", "cap"→"white hard hat"), so the model learns to prefer granular labels and relations.

12) Penalize dataset priors and inference: explicitly instruct the model not to infer counts, roles, ages, or unseen attributes; only claim what is directly visible.

These changes emphasize precise object identity, small props, part‑level interactions, legible text, and one background anchor—features that carry strong CLIP signal and address the recurring failure modes in the critiques.

Summary recommendation: tighten the global caption prompt to force detection and explicit reporting of high‑signal, verifiable visual cues (legible text, micro‑actions, reflections/signage, part‑level interactions, clear spatial anchors) and to eliminate hedging and invented facts. Concrete prompt changes to adopt
1. Require a deterministic spatial anchor rule (centroid and width): compute centroid → emit left/center/right; if subject width >60% image width emit "center"; if subject partly out of frame append exact cropped edge. Do not guess depth unless overlap/size clearly indicates foreground/midground/background.

2. Replace vague action reporting with strict micro‑action rules: include an action phrase only when one of: visible limb‑object contact, object held by hand, visible deformation/pressure, displaced/midair object, clear gaze toward an object, or motion blur on limbs. If none apply, emit exactly "no-action-visible". Define micro‑action phrase formats (e.g., "[hand] [verb] [object]" or "holding [object] with [hand]").

3. Force one high‑signal descriptor slot (up to 3 max) with strict priority: A) legible text (transcribe only if every character is readable; include quoted string and localization), B) reflections/surface condition, C) material/texture, D) distinctive accessory, E) color. Enforce max 3 and drop uncertain candidates.

4. Require one concise part‑level relation when an interaction is visible (format: "[part] [verb] [structure/object]" — e.g., "right hand holding pole", "rear wheel off ground"). Do not invent interactions.

Add verification checks in the prompt: (a) transcribe text only if all chars legible; (b) include count digits only if clearly visible; (c) include depth only if overlap/scale cues exist; (d) include cropped edge only if part of subject is out of frame; (e) drop tokens failing verification and re-evaluate.

8. Keep output format strict and compact: single grammatical sentence, comma‑separated short phrases, ≤30 words (allow +10% only to include legible text or necessary relation/background). Encourage active, factual verbs and concrete nouns to maximize CLIP alignment.

9. Provide a small set (3–5) of tightly constrained examples in the prompt that show correct handling of: storefront reflections vs behind‑glass objects, busker with instrument case and gaze, dancer group with marquee text, surfer with spray arc, and a pillow‑fight mid‑motion — to teach micro‑action, reflections, signage, group arrangement, and motion blur cues.

textgrad_loss_text:
Summary diagnosis
- CLIP scores are low (mean_clip 0.297, negative mean_delta_clip) while SigLIP wins are relatively strong, indicating the prompt yields captions that match some semantic/lexical proxies but miss the most discriminative, CLIP‑sensitive visual tokens (legible text, precise object types, props, part‑level relations).

Concrete, reusable prompt changes (apply across all images)
1. Prioritize transcription and precise object labels
   - Make legible text and exact object class (e.g., "moped", "cargo bike", "motorized scooter" vs. generic "bicycle") the highest priority tokens. CLIP gains most from exact words; require explicit transcription whenever every character is readable (keep current verification), and require concrete vehicle/tool labels when visual evidence supports them.

2. Elevate part‑level relations and contact evidence
   - Move the "part-level relation" token above generic descriptors in the priority ordering. Force inclusion of exactly one contact/interaction phrase whenever there is visible limb‑object contact, tools touching workpieces, or clear displacement (wheel off ground, hand on fruit, instrument to mouth). This yields high-value, discriminative cues for CLIP.

3. Make micro‑action rules stricter and give examples
   - Replace vague "holding" allowances with stricter verification: include a micro‑action only when there is clear contact or functional use (hand on handlebar, instrument at mouth, weighing scale shows coins). Require detection of supporting props (open case, scale) to assert actions like "busking" indirectly via parts.

4. Require explicit, discriminative props and context
   - Add a descriptor category for small but discriminative props (scale, woven baskets with fruit, open instrument case, mounted fish, marquee text). Treat such props on par with legible text and material cues for inclusion priority.

5. Relax exact count rule to avoid harmful false precision
   - Allow "about N" or "N?" phrasing when separation/occlusion makes exact counting uncertain, or prefer "a line of dancers" / "a group of N" guidance. Keep hard digit output only when verification ≥50% unobstructed is met, but provide the captioner a clear fallback wording rule to avoid wrong exact counts (this preserves CLIP compatibility with concrete nouns without hallucinated digits).

6. Expand and clarify descriptor priority list
   - Reorder descriptor priorities to: (A) legible text → (B) part‑level relation/prop → (C) exact object class/vehicle/tool → (D) material/texture → (E) color → (F) reflection/surface condition. This emphasizes tokens CLIP responds to most.

7. Add mandatory small‑detail checks for scenes with vendors/performers/buildings
   - For street/vendor/market scenes: require checking for baskets, scales, fruit, signage, and vehicle type before writing "vendor"/"bike".
   - For performers/parades/theaters: require transcription of marquee/signs if legible, require naming non‑performer figures (Santa, musicians) if visually prominent.

8. Strengthen two‑pass verification and specify thresholds
   - Formalize thresholds developers referenced in critiques: font legibility = characters > 8pt equivalent, high contrast; count verification = ≥50% unobstructed instances; object class = model confidence > threshold (specify internal confidence). If thresholds fail, drop token and recheck grammar.

9. Enforce brevity prioritization with new tie breakers
   - If length limits force removals, use new priority: legible text → part‑level relation/prop → precise object class/vehicle → background anchor → material/texture → viewpoint → lighting. This will push CLIP‑relevant tokens into captions.

10. Give concrete negative rules to avoid weak generic phrasing
    - Forbid sole outputs like "holding" or "no-action-visible" when contact/props are present but unreported. Forbid unqualified "bicycle"/"man"/"building" when a more specific, visually supported label exists.

Implementation notes (operational)
- Provide the captioner model with short visual tests/examples showing when to prefer "moped" vs "bicycle", when to transcribe "Radio City" vs drop text, and examples of acceptable "about N" fallbacks.
- Log which high‑priority tokens are dropped by verification per sample to guide further tuning.

Expected effect
- More frequent inclusion of legible text, precise object classes, props, and contact relations should increase CLIP similarity (fewer generic nouns, more discriminative tokens). The suggested ordering and stricter micro‑action/verification rules preserve grammatical brevity while boosting tokens that CLIP weights heavily.

old_prompt:
Output exactly one concise, information‑dense caption: a single grammatical sentence of comma‑separated short phrases. Use digits for counts only when each instance is clearly visible; do not infer, hedge, paraphrase, or add anything not visually present. Output only that one sentence.

Required phrase ordering (include an item only if visually verifiable; omit unverifiable items). Aim for ≤30 words; allow up to +10% length only to include a fully legible quoted text string or one necessary part‑level relation/background anchor.

1) Start with: [digit] + subject noun(s) + spatial anchor.
   - Spatial anchor rules: compute subject centroid x; if x < 0.33 → "left"; if 0.33 ≤ x ≤ 0.66 → "center"; if x > 0.66 → "right".
   - If subject width >60% image width, emit "center" regardless of centroid.
   - If >5% of subject area lies outside image, append "partially cropped at [top|bottom|left|right]".
   - Add depth token [foreground|midground|background] only if overlap/relative scale unambiguously indicates depth.

2) Include exactly one micro‑action phrase only if clear functional contact or use is visually evident (visible limb‑object contact, instrument at mouth, object midair, visible deformation/pressure, motion blur on a limb, or clear gaze at a visible object). Use one of these templates:
   - "[hand] [verb] [object]" (e.g., "right hand holding pole")
   - "holding [object] with [hand]" (e.g., "holding violin with chin and right hand")
   - "[body_part] [verb] [structure/object]" (e.g., "left foot on pedal")
   - If no such clear contact/use is verifiable, omit the micro‑action token (do not print filler phrases).

3) Immediately after micro‑action, include exactly one part‑level relation or contact phrase whenever any limb/object contact, tool touching workpiece, or displacement is visually evident; use the template "[part] [verb] [object/structure]" (e.g., "right hand holding pole", "rear wheel off ground"). If no contact is present, omit this clause.

4) Then include up to 1–3 high‑signal descriptor(s) chosen by strict priority (pick the highest‑ranked verifiable candidates; break ties lexicographically). Priority order:
   A) Fully legible text — transcribe exact string only if every character is clearly readable; include it in quotes and localize (e.g., "'RADIO CITY' on marquee above").
   B) Discriminative prop / part‑level prop (weighing scale, open instrument case, woven baskets with fruit, mounted fish, marquee).
   C) Precise object class (prefer "moped", "cargo bike", "motorized scooter", "bicycle with basket", "surveillance camera", etc., over generic labels).
   D) Material/texture (e.g., "rusted metal", "woven straw").
   E) Color (e.g., "red sweatshirt").
   F) Reflection/surface condition (e.g., "wet pavement with reflections", "glass reflections").
   - Enforce ≤3 descriptors; if none verifiable, omit descriptors.

5) Optionally include exactly one viewpoint token when obvious: {close-up, medium, wide, high-angle, low-angle}.

6) Optionally include exactly one lighting token when obvious: {backlit, front-lit, rim-lit, long-shadow-left, long-shadow-right}.

7) If a clear background anchor is visible, append one concise background noun phrase (single phrase, e.g., "storefront window", "stone embankment", "Radio City marquee"). Omit if no clear anchor.

Reflections vs. behind‑glass rule
- If an element appears doubled, reversed, or overlayed on the glass plane without 3D occlusion → label as "reflections".
- If objects clearly sit on the far side of the glass (shelf, mannequin, handbags) → label as "on display behind glass" or "behind glass".
- If uncertain, omit both.

Two‑pass verification (run before emitting)
a) Text transcription: transcribe quoted text only if every character is clearly readable (high contrast, character size equivalent ≳8pt at image scale). If full string is not readable, do not invent text; instead include sign presence/localization as a descriptor (e.g., "marquee above") if position is clear.
b) Count verification: include a digit only if each instance is ≥50% unobstructed and separable; otherwise use a descriptive phrase (e.g., "a line of dancers", "a group of people") rather than an incorrect digit.
c) Object class verification: include a fine class only if internal object confidence >0.60 (or top label margin >0.15); otherwise fall back to the next specific supported class or generic class only if nothing specific is verifiable.
d) Contact verification: require visible occlusion/adjacency or clear overlapping pixels to assert limb‑object contact or tool interaction.
e) If any token fails verification, drop that token and recheck sentence for grammaticality.

Brevity & trimming priorities
- If length limits force removal, prioritize tokens in this order: legible text → part‑level relation / discriminative prop → precise object class → background anchor → material/texture → viewpoint → lighting → color → reflection.
- Prefer compact, active, factual phrasing and concrete nouns. Do not infer ages, emotions, roles, intent, or unseen attributes. Do not use vague quantifiers ("several","many") — use digits only when verified.

Negative rules
- Do not output a generic label (e.g., "bicycle", "man", "building") if a more specific, visually supported label is available.
- Do not state exact counts when verification fails.
- Do not emit micro‑action claims (e.g., "holding") unless contact/use is clearly visible.

Style constraints
- Single sentence, comma‑separated short phrases, no tags, no lists, no extra lines.
- Use canonical labels (e.g., "storefront window", "center"), consistent punctuation for quoted text.
- Maintain grammaticality after dropping any failed tokens.

Canonical minute examples (follow exact output format):
- "1 child left foreground, right hand reaching toward storefront window, right hand touching glass, 'LOEWE' on lower sill at left, glass reflections, storefront window behind."
- "1 woman center foreground, holding violin with chin and right hand, open instrument case on ground, medium, tiled underground passage behind."
- "5 dancers center foreground, standing in long line across crosswalk, red and white striped costumes, Radio City marquee above, street behind."

Follow these rules exactly to produce one precise caption.
new_prompt:
Output exactly one concise, information‑dense caption: a single grammatical sentence composed of comma‑separated short phrases. Produce only that one sentence (no lists, tags, JSON, logs, or extra lines). Use digits for counts only when each instance is clearly visible and separable; do not infer, hedge, or invent unseen attributes.

General structure and group allowance
- Allow 1–3 clearly separable subject groups in prominence order. For each group, emit: [digit] + subject noun(s) + spatial anchor. Include a group only if it passes per-group verification (see "Group inclusion" below). Keep overall brevity; include a secondary group only if it occupies ≥20% of the main subject area or is visually prominent.

Spatial anchor and grouping rules
- Compute a centroid per subject/group. If centroid x < 0.33 → "left"; if 0.33 ≤ x ≤ 0.66 → "center"; if x > 0.66 → "right".
- If a subject width >50% of image width, emit "center" for that subject.
- If >5% of subject area lies outside image, append "partially cropped at [top|bottom|left|right]".
- Add depth token [foreground|midground|background] only if overlap/relative scale unambiguously indicates depth.
- In multi‑group scenes compute centroid per group rather than collapsing to a single centroid.

Micro‑action and contact (strict, verbized)
- Include exactly one micro‑action phrase only if clear functional contact/use is visually evident (visible limb‑object contact, instrument at mouth, object midair, visible deformation/pressure, motion blur on a limb, or clear gaze at a visible object).
- The micro‑action must be verbized (e.g., "right hand inserting screwdriver", "left hand holding leash"). Do not use passive or vague forms like "with" unless required by a template ("holding [object] with [hand]").
- Contact verification: assert contact only if bounding‑box intersection ≥10–15% of the smaller bbox OR visible pixel overlap/segmentation adjacency OR clear edge adjacency; otherwise drop micro‑action.
- If contact is verified, immediately include exactly one part‑level relation using the template "[part] [verb] [object/structure]" (e.g., "right hand holding pole", "rear wheel off ground"). If no verified contact, omit both micro‑action and part‑level relation.

Descriptor selection and priority (≤3 descriptors)
- Choose up to 1–3 high‑signal descriptors after the subject/micro‑action/part relation. Priority (highest → lowest):
  1) Discriminative prop or part‑level prop (weigh these first: open instrument case, woven baskets with fruit, satellite dish, marquee).
  2) Precise object class (prefer "moped", "cargo bike", "surveillance camera", "bicycle with basket" over generic labels).
  3) Fully legible text (transcribe exact string only if every character is clearly readable).
  4) Material/texture (rusted metal, woven straw).
  5) Color (red sweatshirt).
  6) Reflection/surface condition (wet pavement with reflections).
- Enforce ≤3 descriptors; if none pass verification, omit descriptors.

Viewpoint, lighting, background anchor (optional but preferred)
- Optionally include at most one viewpoint token when obvious: {close-up, medium, wide, high-angle, low-angle}.
- Optionally include at most one lighting token when obvious: {backlit, front-lit, rim-lit, long-shadow-left, long-shadow-right}.
- If a clear background anchor is visible (occupies ≥5% image area or is a distinct structure), append one concise background noun phrase (e.g., "storefront window", "stone embankment", "parapet with satellite dishes"). If no clear anchor, omit.

Reflections vs. behind‑glass (procedural)
- If an element appears doubled, reversed, or overlayed on the glass plane without 3D occlusion → label as "reflections".
- If objects clearly sit on the far side of glass with supporting occlusion by a display plane (shelves, mannequins, items behind visible glass frame) → label as "on display behind glass" or "behind glass".
- If uncertain, omit both.

Two‑pass verification (mandatory)
1) Propose tokens for each slot (groups, micro‑action, part relation, descriptors, viewpoint, lighting, background).
2) Verify tokens with these numeric checks:
   - Count: include a digit only if each instance is ≥50% unobstructed and separable.
   - Object class: require classifier confidence >0.60 OR top-label margin >0.15; if confidence scores are unavailable, require multiple visual cues or distinctive parts before asserting a fine class.
   - Contact: require bbox overlap ≥10–15% of smaller bbox OR segmentation adjacency/clear pixel overlap.
   - Text: transcribe quoted text only if each character is clearly readable at ≳8pt equivalent and high contrast; otherwise use a position/label descriptor (e.g., "marquee above").
3) If any token fails verification, drop it and recheck grammaticality. Always ensure the final sentence remains grammatical after any drops.

Mandatory checks to improve grounding
- If any discriminative prop or verified part‑level relation exists per the verification rules, the caption must include at least one such token (pick the highest‑priority verified token).
- If two or more verified subjects are present and any clear interaction (handing, facing, next to, gaze) or relative placement is unambiguous, include a short inter‑subject relation token (e.g., "facing", "handing", "next to").

Pose/orientation and object state (when unambiguous)
- When clearly visible, include one brief orientation token for subjects: {facing camera, turned away, leaning over, crouching, walking toward camera}.
- When object state is visibly informative, include one object‑state descriptor: {open instrument case, exposed gears, wet reflective surface, broken panel}.

Brevity and trimming priorities
- Aim for ≤30 words; allow up to +10% length only to include a fully legible quoted text string or one necessary part‑level relation/background anchor.
- If trimming is required, prioritize tokens to keep in this order (highest→lowest): discriminative prop → part‑level relation/contact → precise object class → background anchor → fully legible text → material/texture → viewpoint → lighting → color → reflection.
- Prefer compact, active phrasing (verb + noun) and concrete nouns. Do not infer ages, emotions, intentions, or unseen attributes. Do not use vague quantifiers ("several") — use digits only when verified.

Negative rules (must obey)
- Do not output a generic label if a more specific, visually supported label is available.
- Do not state exact counts when verification fails.
- Do not emit micro‑action claims (e.g., "holding") unless contact is clearly verified.
- Do not invent text or partial transcriptions; only transcribe when fully legible.

Canonical compact templates (follow format; these are templates to emulate)
- "1 child left foreground, right hand inserting screwdriver, right hand touching mechanism, open metal case on table, medium, workshop bench behind."
- "2 men center foreground, facing each other, left man handing packet, brown woven basket with fruit, low parapet with satellite dishes behind."
- "1 dog right foreground, walking left, long legs and tucked waist, wet pavement with reflections, low-angle, street behind."

Final note
- Maintain the single‑sentence, comma‑separated output style exactly. Verify tokens via the two‑pass checks and ensure at least one discriminative prop or part relation is present when visually supported. Prioritize concrete objects, actions, and verified relations to maximize visual grounding in a single concise caption.

textgrad_loss_text:
Summary: the current rigid, single‑sentence schema yields non‑aligned captions (mean CLIP ≈0.30, negative delta), because it often omits other visible people/animals, interactions, discriminative props, precise object classes, and explicit action/contact—features that CLIP strongly weights. Make these reusable prompt fixes.

Recommended prompt changes (concise, actionable)

1) Allow multiple visible subject groups at the start
   - Change the opening constraint from a single “[digit] + subject noun(s) + spatial anchor” to permit listing one or more clearly separable subject groups in prominence order (e.g., “1 man left foreground, 2 women right midground, …”), each following the same centroid/width/area verification rules. This prevents eliding additional visible people/animals.

2) Require explicit interaction/relative placement
   - Add an instruction to describe interactions between visible subjects (handing/receiving, facing, looking at, next to, behind) and to give relative placement (left/right/center and depth when unambiguous). Prioritize including such interaction verbs if they are visually evident.

3) Promote discriminative props and fine object classes
   - Raise the priority of discriminative props and precise object classes (props B and class C) above color/texture. Instruct the model to prefer naming a specific prop or fine class over generic labels or colors when visual evidence meets verification thresholds.

4) Enforce verbized micro‑actions and strict contact verification
   - Keep the single micro‑action token rule but require a verb form (e.g., “right hand inserting screwdriver”) and mandate pixel‑level overlap/occlusion or clear adjacency per two‑pass contact verification before asserting contact. If contact is present, require the part‑level relation immediately after (no optional omission).

5) Strengthen two‑pass verification thresholds and procedures
   - Clarify and tighten verification: counts only if each instance ≥50% unobstructed and separable; object class only if confidence >0.60 or top-label margin >0.15; contact only with clear overlapping pixels; quoted text only if every character legible per existing rule. If a token fails, drop it and re-run grammaticality check.

6) Require salient scene anchors and environment tokens when present
   - Explicitly require one salient background anchor or scene object (storefront, parapet, satellite dish, instrument case, boxes) when clearly visible, and require mentioning lighting/reflection cues (flash, wet pavement with reflections, glass reflections) when obvious—these often increase CLIP alignment.

7) Capture pose/orientation and object state
   - Add a short required clause when applicable: subject orientation (turned away, facing camera, leaning over) and object state (open instrument case, exposed gears, wet reflective surface). These fine details are high‑value features for CLIP.

8) Reorder trimming priorities toward content that boosts visual grounding
   - When trimming length, prefer to keep (1) discriminative props, (2) part‑level relations/contact, (3) precise object class, (4) background anchor, (5) legible text, then material/texture, viewpoint, lighting, color, reflection. (This reorders the current emphasis to favor concrete objects/relations.)

9) Relax or clarify spatial-anchor heuristics for wide or grouped subjects
   - Keep centroid thresholds but explicitly handle wide subjects and multi‑group scenes: if multiple distinct groups exist, compute centroid per group; if subject width >50–60% keep “center” but permit group enumeration to avoid collapsing scene into a single subject.

10) Compactness rules: prefer verbs and nouns over adjectives
    - Emphasize compact, active phrasing (verb + noun) and prefer naming objects and actions over colors/adjectives unless those adjectives are discriminative props. This reduces filler and increases CLIP-relevant content.

11) Maintain exact transcription checks but deprioritize rare text over props
    - Keep the strict transcription rule for quoted text, but do not let the presence/absence of fully legible text block inclusion of higher‑value visual tokens (props, actions).

Implementation note
- Make these changes explicit in the prompt as short verification checkpoints and a revised token importance list; add one mandatory pass that ensures at least one discriminative prop or part‑level relation is included when visually present. These changes are minimally invasive to the current format but shift priority toward the objects, actions, contacts, and scene anchors that drive CLIP similarity.

Output exactly one concise, information‑dense caption: a single grammatical sentence composed of comma‑separated short phrases. Produce only that one sentence (no lists, tags, JSON, logs, or extra lines). Use digits for counts only when each instance is clearly visible and separable; do not infer, hedge, or invent unseen attributes.

General structure and group allowance
- Allow 1–3 clearly separable subject groups in prominence order. For each group, emit: [digit] + subject noun(s) + spatial anchor. Include a group only if it passes per-group verification (see "Group inclusion" below). Keep overall brevity; include a secondary group only if it occupies ≥20% of the main subject area or is visually prominent.

Spatial anchor and grouping rules
- Compute a centroid per subject/group. If centroid x < 0.33 → "left"; if 0.33 ≤ x ≤ 0.66 → "center"; if x > 0.66 → "right".
- If a subject width >50% of image width, emit "center" for that subject.
- If >5% of subject area lies outside image, append "partially cropped at [top|bottom|left|right]".
- Add depth token [foreground|midground|background] only if overlap/relative scale unambiguously indicates depth.
- In multi‑group scenes compute centroid per group rather than collapsing to a single centroid.

Micro‑action and contact (strict, verbized)
- Include exactly one micro‑action phrase only if clear functional contact/use is visually evident (visible limb‑object contact, instrument at mouth, object midair, visible deformation/pressure, motion blur on a limb, or clear gaze at a visible object).
- The micro‑action must be verbized (e.g., "right hand inserting screwdriver", "left hand holding leash"). Do not use passive or vague forms like "with" unless required by a template ("holding [object] with [hand]").
- Contact verification: assert contact only if bounding‑box intersection ≥10–15% of the smaller bbox OR visible pixel overlap/segmentation adjacency OR clear edge adjacency; otherwise drop micro‑action.
- If contact is verified, immediately include exactly one part‑level relation using the template "[part] [verb] [object/structure]" (e.g., "right hand holding pole", "rear wheel off ground"). If no verified contact, omit both micro‑action and part‑level relation.

Descriptor selection and priority (≤3 descriptors)
- Choose up to 1–3 high‑signal descriptors after the subject/micro‑action/part relation. Priority (highest → lowest):
  1) Discriminative prop or part‑level prop (weigh these first: open instrument case, woven baskets with fruit, satellite dish, marquee).
  2) Precise object class (prefer "moped", "cargo bike", "surveillance camera", "bicycle with basket" over generic labels).
  3) Fully legible text (transcribe exact string only if every character is clearly readable).
  4) Material/texture (rusted metal, woven straw).
  5) Color (red sweatshirt).
  6) Reflection/surface condition (wet pavement with reflections).
- Enforce ≤3 descriptors; if none pass verification, omit descriptors.

Viewpoint, lighting, background anchor (optional but preferred)
- Optionally include at most one viewpoint token when obvious: {close-up, medium, wide, high-angle, low-angle}.
- Optionally include at most one lighting token when obvious: {backlit, front-lit, rim-lit, long-shadow-left, long-shadow-right}.
- If a clear background anchor is visible (occupies ≥5% image area or is a distinct structure), append one concise background noun phrase (e.g., "storefront window", "stone embankment", "parapet with satellite dishes"). If no clear anchor, omit.

Reflections vs. behind‑glass (procedural)
- If an element appears doubled, reversed, or overlayed on the glass plane without 3D occlusion → label as "reflections".
- If objects clearly sit on the far side of glass with supporting occlusion by a display plane (shelves, mannequins, items behind visible glass frame) → label as "on display behind glass" or "behind glass".
- If uncertain, omit both.

Two‑pass verification (mandatory)
1) Propose tokens for each slot (groups, micro‑action, part relation, descriptors, viewpoint, lighting, background).
2) Verify tokens with these numeric checks:
   - Count: include a digit only if each instance is ≥50% unobstructed and separable.
   - Object class: require classifier confidence >0.60 OR top-label margin >0.15; if confidence scores are unavailable, require multiple visual cues or distinctive parts before asserting a fine class.
   - Contact: require bbox overlap ≥10–15% of smaller bbox OR segmentation adjacency/clear pixel overlap.
   - Text: transcribe quoted text only if each character is clearly readable at ≳8pt equivalent and high contrast; otherwise use a position/label descriptor (e.g., "marquee above").
3) If any token fails verification, drop it and recheck grammaticality. Always ensure the final sentence remains grammatical after any drops.

Mandatory checks to improve grounding
- If any discriminative prop or verified part‑level relation exists per the verification rules, the caption must include at least one such token (pick the highest‑priority verified token).
- If two or more verified subjects are present and any clear interaction (handing, facing, next to, gaze) or relative placement is unambiguous, include a short inter‑subject relation token (e.g., "facing", "handing", "next to").

Pose/orientation and object state (when unambiguous)
- When clearly visible, include one brief orientation token for subjects: {facing camera, turned away, leaning over, crouching, walking toward camera}.
- When object state is visibly informative, include one object‑state descriptor: {open instrument case, exposed gears, wet reflective surface, broken panel}.

Brevity and trimming priorities
- Aim for ≤30 words; allow up to +10% length only to include a fully legible quoted text string or one necessary part‑level relation/background anchor.
- If trimming is required, prioritize tokens to keep in this order (highest→lowest): discriminative prop → part‑level relation/contact → precise object class → background anchor → fully legible text → material/texture → viewpoint → lighting → color → reflection.
- Prefer compact, active phrasing (verb + noun) and concrete nouns. Do not infer ages, emotions, intentions, or unseen attributes. Do not use vague quantifiers ("several") — use digits only when verified.

Negative rules (must obey)
- Do not output a generic label if a more specific, visually supported label is available.
- Do not state exact counts when verification fails.
- Do not emit micro‑action claims (e.g., "holding") unless contact is clearly verified.
- Do not invent text or partial transcriptions; only transcribe when fully legible.

Canonical compact templates (follow format; these are templates to emulate)
- "1 child left foreground, right hand inserting screwdriver, right hand touching mechanism, open metal case on table, medium, workshop bench behind."
- "2 men center foreground, facing each other, left man handing packet, brown woven basket with fruit, low parapet with satellite dishes behind."
- "1 dog right foreground, walking left, long legs and tucked waist, wet pavement with reflections, low-angle, street behind."

Final note
- Maintain the single‑sentence, comma‑separated output style exactly. Verify tokens via the two‑pass checks and ensure at least one discriminative prop or part relation is present when visually supported. Prioritize concrete objects, actions, and verified relations to maximize visual grounding in a single concise caption.

1) Token proposal: internally list candidate tokens for each slot — groups, micro‑action, part relation, up to three descriptors, viewpoint, lighting, background/text.

- Background anchor: include a background noun phrase only if that anchor occupies ≥5% image area or is a distinct structure.
- If classifier/confidence metadata is unavailable, require at least two independent visual cues before asserting fine classes; otherwise use a higher‑level class.

- Include exactly one verbized micro‑action only if Contact verification passes. Use a strong verb (e.g., "holding", "inserting", "walking") and immediately follow with one part‑level relation using the exact template: "[part] [verb] [object]" (e.g., "right hand holding pole"). - Do not use passive or vague forms; do not use "with" except inside the required template.

- Choose at most three verified descriptors in this strict priority order: (1) discriminative prop or part‑level prop, (2) precise object class, (3) fully legible text (quoted), (4) material/texture, (5) color, (6) reflection/surface condition. If none verify, omit descriptors.

Background, signage and reflections
- If text is fully legible per Text verification, quote exact string. Otherwise use a positional label (e.g., "signboard above", "storefront window").
- If an element appears doubled/reversed on a glass plane without 3D occlusion, label it "reflections". If items clearly sit behind glass with supporting occlusion, label "on display behind glass". If uncertain, omit both.

- When unambiguous, include one brief orientation token (e.g., "facing camera", "turned away", "leaning over").
- When object state is clearly visible, include one object‑state descriptor (e.g., "open instrument case", "wet reflective surface").

Mandatory high‑signal inclusion
- If any discriminative prop or verified part‑level relation passes verification, the caption must include at least one such token (priority: prop > part relation > precise class).

Trimming priority (deterministic checklist)
- If over length, deterministically drop tokens in this order until within limit: color → viewpoint → lighting → reflections → material/texture → quoted text (unless necessary) → background (unless ≥5% area or necessary) → low‑priority descriptors. Always preserve discriminative prop and verified part relation when present.

Negative rules (must obey)
- Do not output multiple candidates or meta information.
- Do not invent counts, contacts, text, or fine classes that fail verification.

- Good: "2 men center foreground, facing each other, left man handing packet, brown woven basket with fruit, storefront behind."
- Bad (avoid): "several people near a sign" — (vague count and sign).
- Bad (avoid): "man holding something" — (no verified contact or object).

- Always perform the two‑pass proposal + verification + pruning process, then emit exactly one grammatical comma‑separated sentence that preserves verified discriminative props and part relations where available and stays within the word limit.

  image_relpath: images/flickr30k/flickr30k_test_000403.jpg

textgrad_loss_text:
Summary recommendations to tighten the global captioning prompt for better CLIP grounding

- Enforce and operationalize verification thresholds explicitly: require digit counts only if ≥50% unobstructed and separable; require fine‑class labels only if classifier confidence >0.60 or multiple unambiguous visual cues; require contact only if bbox overlap ≥12% of the smaller box or clear segmentation adjacency; require text transcription only if ≳8pt equivalent and high contrast. If a token fails its check, drop it and revalidate the sentence for grammaticality.

- Make discriminative props and verified part‑level relations mandatory tokens whenever present and verified; prioritize generating at least one such token per caption (prop > part relation > precise class) to increase CLIP alignment.

- Tighten micro‑action rules and phrasing: insist on a single verbized micro‑action only when contact verification passes; immediately follow it with one explicit part‑level relation using the exact template; otherwise omit both. Use strong action verbs (leap/jump/insert/hold/walk) for motion and orientation tokens.

- Require explicit, localized group composition and spatial relations: ask the model to produce 1–3 subject groups in prominence order with centroid‑based anchors (left/center/right) and add depth tokens only when scale/overlap unambiguously indicate depth. If a subject spans >50% image width, force "center".

- Increase emphasis on concrete, high‑signal descriptors (≤3) in this priority order: discriminative prop → precise object class → fully legible text → material/texture → color → reflection. Drop vague descriptors and forbid inferred attributes (no age/emotion/intention).

- Strengthen background/signage handling: transcribe text only when fully legible; otherwise require a positional label (e.g., "marquee above", "storefront window") and encourage noting distinctive architectural or scene anchors that occupy ≥5% area.

- Shorten and standardize length: target ≤24 words (hard cap ~27), using the existing trimming priority to drop lower‑value tokens first (color, viewpoint, lighting). Favor compact comma‑separated noun‑verb phrases and preserve the required template order (groups → micro‑action/part → descriptors → viewpoint/lighting → background).

- Add a mandatory two‑pass generation procedure in the prompt: (1) propose all tokens for slots, (2) apply the numeric verification checks and prune failing tokens, then render a single grammatical comma‑separated sentence. Make this explicit so the model self‑validates instead of guessing.

- Provide explicit examples of accepted vs. rejected token formations (short canonical cases) so the model learns to prefer concrete props, verified contacts, and precise spatial anchors over hedged or vague language.

These changes concentrate probability mass on verified concrete nouns, part relations, and discriminative props—features that empirically raise CLIP image/text alignment—while preserving the current structural constraints and verification rigor.

Summary: the prompt yields terse but non‑discriminative captions that reduce CLIP alignment (low mean_clip, negative delta_clip, low clip_win_rate). Change the global prompt to force more verifiable, distinctive visual tokens and stricter verification heuristics so captions anchor on the elements CLIP cares about (props, legible text, precise object classes, spatial relations).

Concrete, reusable prompt changes

- Raise discriminative props/text to the top priority and require one when present: mandate inclusion of a verified prop (unique object, container, tool, sign text) before lower‑value descriptors. Define “present” by the verification rules (classifier confidence >0.60 OR two independent visual cues).

- Strengthen fine‑class fallback rules: when classifier confidences are unavailable, require two independent visual cues (distinctive part + unique shape OR part + contextual prop) before asserting a fine class (e.g., “motorbike” vs “bicycle”). Provide concrete cue examples in the prompt (wheels+engine+exhaust = motorbike; pedals+spokes+chain = bicycle).

- Make text handling explicit and strict: transcribe and quote only when fully legible at ≳8pt and high contrast; otherwise require a positional label (e.g., “signboard above”, “doorway text at left”). Add an instruction to call out partially legible or painted text as “painted text on shutter” rather than guessing words.

- Enforce stronger contact/micro‑action verification: only emit a verbized micro‑action and the required “[part] [verb] [object]” relation when bbox overlap ≥12% of the smaller bbox OR segmentation adjacency is clear. Supply this as a hard gating rule and give two short examples in the prompt so the model learns to omit micro‑actions when contact is ambiguous.

- Make spatial anchors and cropping deterministic: require centroid x and subject width checks as the sole source for left/center/right and “partially cropped at …” tags, and require including depth only when scale/occlusion is unambiguous. This reduces vague placement words that hurt CLIP alignment.

- Prefer concrete background anchors over generic materials: instruct the model to call out storefronts, signage, architectural features and their position (e.g., “storefront behind”, “metal shutter with horizontal slats”) when the background occupies ≥5% image area or contains legible text. Discourage generic labels like “brick wall” unless that is the only identifiable anchor.

- Tighten descriptor priority and trimming: move quoted text and discriminative prop above material/color/viewpoint; when over length, deterministically drop color then viewpoint then lighting, always preserving verified props and verified part relations.

- Make count and saliency rules explicit and conservative: allow digits only when each instance is ≥50% unobstructed and separable; include guidance to estimate separability (distinct silhouettes/spacing). For secondary groups require ≥20% area of main subject or top‑2 saliency bin.

- Add short examples showing good vs bad phrasing tailored to CLIP: good = specific prop + location + verified micro‑action; bad = vague person labels or unsourced actions. Include one example that demonstrates preferring “motorbike with baskets attached” only when two cues verify motorbike.

- Diagnostic logging instruction for developers (internal use): have the model emit (internally) which verification checks passed for each chosen token so later debugging can correlate which rules drop high‑value tokens; do not expose these logs in captions.

Net effect: these changes force the model to favor precise, verifiable, high‑signal tokens (props, text, fine classes when backed by cues, part relations when contact is clear) and to drop low‑value fluff (unsourced actions, vague backgrounds, unverified colors), which should increase CLIP image–text similarity without changing the required single‑sentence, comma‑separated output format.

Numeric verification rules (deterministic)
- Count: include a digit only if each instance is ≥50% unobstructed and individually separable. Separability = (centroid spacing ≥10% image width) AND (IOU between subject bboxes <0.10). If either fails, omit digits and emit a generic singular/plural group without numbers.
- Contact (micro‑action): assert contact only if overlap area / smaller bbox area ≥12% AND segmentation/pixel adjacency supports true touch (distinguish hand-to-person vs hand-to-glass by contiguous skin pixels or visible arm through window). Always specify which part (left/right) when emitting micro‑actions. If contact not verified, omit both micro‑action and part relation.
- Fine object class: emit a fine class only if classifier confidence >0.60 OR a matching explicit cue‑pair (see cue‑pair table). If metadata unavailable, require the cue‑pair. Do not invent fine classes otherwise.
- Text transcription: quote exact text only if fully legible at ≳8pt equivalent and high contrast; otherwise emit a positional label ("painted text on shutter at left", "phone number on board at center") and include dominant sign color/shape when legible transcription fails.

Cue‑pair templates (explicit, implementable)
- Mug/thermos: (handle + open top) OR (cylindrical body + metal rim/lid).  
- Ladder: (visible rungs + side rails) OR (rungs + ladder leaning against vertical structure).  
- Jackfruit/produce: (spiky rind + large yellow flesh) OR (leaf bed + multiple cut pieces).  
- Vendor: (baskets/piles of produce + countertop/table) OR (scale/pans + transaction posture).  
- Dog touching person: (paw bbox overlapping human limb bbox ≥12%) OR (continuous pixels showing paw contacting arm/hand).  
- Car/window interaction: (open window + person arm visible through opening) OR (hand overlapping person inside bbox ≥12%).  
- Bicycle: (pedals + chain) OR (spokes + visible pedals).  
- Motorbike: (engine casing + exhaust) OR (frame + visible exhaust).

- Include one orientation token when unambiguous by measurable cues (e.g., symmetrical face orientation, torso angle): "facing camera", "turned away", "leaning over". Include one object‑state descriptor when clearly visible (e.g., "open instrument case", "wet reflective surface").

Deterministic tie‑breakers
- If two subjects have similar prominence, choose the one with larger bbox area. If bbox areas tie, choose the leftmost centroid. If subject width >50% image width → emit "center". Append "partially cropped at [top|bottom|left|right]" if >5% of subject area lies outside the image.

- If text verified per Text rule, quote exact string. If not, emit a positional label and include dominant sign color/shape (e.g., "painted white phone number on blue board at center"). Label reflections explicitly only when doubled/reversed on glass; otherwise prefer neutral positional phrasing.

Count & saliency rules
- Allow digits only when Count verification passes. Include a secondary subject group only if it covers ≥20% of main subject area OR ranks top‑2 by area/saliency. When saliency metadata unavailable, use area thresholds.

- If classifier confidence or cue‑pairs fail, ban unverifiable fine‑class tokens and instead use neutral but concrete descriptors (e.g., "metal container", "folded paper"). Do not invent specifics. Do not output vague quantifiers like "several".

- Bad: "dog near car" → Good: "1 small white dog center foreground, mid‑jump paw contacting passenger hand through open window of silver car."  
- Bad: "bike" (uncertain) → Good: "1 man right foreground, standing by bicycle with visible pedals and chain, storefront behind."

Mandatory generation procedure (two‑pass)

Required overall format & hard limits

Each group: [digit if verified] + subject noun(s) + spatial anchor (left/center/right) and optional depth token only when depth verification passes. Target ≤24 words; allow up to +10% (≤27 words) only to include a fully legible quoted text string or one necessary verified part‑relation or background anchor. Use active, compressed noun‑verb phrases.

Numeric verification rules (deterministic)
- Count: include a digit only if each instance is ≥50% unobstructed and individually separable. Separability = (centroid spacing ≥10% image width) AND (IOU between subject bboxes <0.10). If either fails, omit digits and emit a generic singular/plural group without numbers.
- Contact (micro‑action): assert contact only if overlap area / smaller bbox area ≥12% AND segmentation/pixel adjacency supports true touch (distinguish hand-to-person vs hand-to-glass by contiguous skin pixels or visible arm through window). If contact verified, include exactly one verbized micro‑action and one part relation using the template: "[left|right] [hand/foot/part] [verb] [object]" (e.g., "right hand holding pole"). Always specify which part (left/right) when emitting micro‑actions. If contact not verified, omit both micro‑action and part relation.

- Text transcription: quote exact text only if fully legible at ≳8pt equivalent and high contrast; otherwise emit a positional label ("painted text on shutter at left", "phone number on board at center") and include dominant sign color/shape when legible transcription fails.
- Background anchor: include a background noun phrase only when that anchor occupies ≥5% image area OR is a distinct structure (storefront, stairway, metal shutter). Use compact phrases (e.g., "storefront behind", "metal shutter at left").

Cue‑pair templates (explicit, implementable)
- Mug/thermos: (handle + open top) OR (cylindrical body + metal rim/lid).  
- Ladder: (visible rungs + side rails) OR (rungs + ladder leaning against vertical structure).  
- Jackfruit/produce: (spiky rind + large yellow flesh) OR (leaf bed + multiple cut pieces).  
- Vendor: (baskets/piles of produce + countertop/table) OR (scale/pans + transaction posture).  
- Dog touching person: (paw bbox overlapping human limb bbox ≥12%) OR (continuous pixels showing paw contacting arm/hand).  
- Car/window interaction: (open window + person arm visible through opening) OR (hand overlapping person inside bbox ≥12%).  
- Bicycle: (pedals + chain) OR (spokes + visible pedals).  
- Motorbike: (engine casing + exhaust) OR (frame + visible exhaust).

Descriptor selection & priority (up to 1–3)

If any discriminative prop or verified part‑relation passes verification, it is mandatory and must be preserved in the final sentence (protected from pruning).

Micro‑action & part‑relation rules (strict)
- Include exactly one micro‑action only if Contact verification passes. Use the exact template: "[left|right] [part] [verb] [object]" (e.g., "right hand holding mug"). Do not use "with" except inside this template. Use a strong verb; avoid passive or vague forms.

Pose/orientation & object state
- Include one orientation token when unambiguous by measurable cues (e.g., symmetrical face orientation, torso angle): "facing camera", "turned away", "leaning over". Include one object‑state descriptor when clearly visible (e.g., "open instrument case", "wet reflective surface").

- If over length, deterministically drop tokens in this order until within limit: color → viewpoint/orientation → lighting → reflections → material/texture → background (unless ≥5% area or contains legible text) → low‑priority descriptors. Never drop a verified discriminative prop or a verified part relation. When tokens tie in priority, remove the one with lower brevity value (longer word cost). Deterministic tie‑breakers
- If two subjects have similar prominence, choose the one with larger bbox area. If bbox areas tie, choose the leftmost centroid. If subject width >50% image width → emit "center". Append "partially cropped at [top|bottom|left|right]" if >5% of subject area lies outside the image.

High-level goal: make the global prompt force concise, verifiable, and discriminative captions that front‑load concrete visual tokens (props, text, object class cues, pose) and avoid hallucination — this will raise CLIP image–text alignment.

Recommended prompt changes (actionable, reusable)

1. Add explicit verification rules the captioner must run before emitting tokens:
   - Count: require ≥50% unobstructed instances, centroid spacing ≥10% image width, IOU <0.10 to emit a digit; otherwise use singular/plural.
   - Contact: require overlap area ≥12% of smaller bbox AND visible attachment/contiguous boundary to emit a contact micro‑action (template: "left/right hand/foot part strong‑verb object").
   - Fine class cue‑pairs: list required cue pairs for vendor, bicycle, motorbike, ladder, performer; if cue‑pair fails, force a defined fallback noun (e.g., "woven basket", "two‑wheeled vehicle", "minivan", "storefront", "cart").
   - OCR: quote text only when OCR confidence high AND text bbox ≥0.5% image area AND legibility high; otherwise emit compact positional sign descriptor with dominant color/shape.

2. Require front‑loading and preservation of VERIFIED tokens:
   - VERIFIED discriminative props, fine classes, and part relations must appear within the first 6–8 words and may not be pruned.
   - Provide a strict descriptor priority list to preserve during pruning: (1) verified props/text, (2) verified part relations, (3) verified fine class, (4) clothing/pose/gaze, (5) object state/material, (6) viewpoint/orientation, (7) color, (8) lighting/reflection.

3. Enforce strict grammatical/formatting template:
   - Single grammatical sentence composed of comma‑separated short phrases.
   - Emit 1–3 subject groups in prominence order with required placement phrases (left/center/right and foreground/background only if depth verified).
   - Target 10–14 words, hard cap 18 (allow extension only when quoting verified text). Provide deterministic pruning order: color → material → reflections → lighting → background → low‑priority descriptors.

4. Micro‑action and motion policy:
   - Only use dynamic verbs or contact verbs when Contact VERIFIED; otherwise avoid motion verbs or imply static poses (use "standing", "walking" only if motion evidence verified).
   - If contact verified, include exactly one micro‑action using the left/right template; always specify left/right.

5. Composition & pose requirements:
   - When a human is present, require one precise pose/orientation token (e.g., "profile mid‑stride", "seated", "diving left") if clear.
   - Require small-object transcription (e.g., ball, phone, bottle) by material/shape if visible and not occluded.

6. Background and signage rules:
   - Include background anchor only if background occupies ≥5% image area or is a distinct structure (storefront, shutter, marquee); otherwise omit.
   - When text is legible per OCR rule, quote exact text; otherwise include compact sign descriptor with dominant color and location.

7. Anti‑hallucination fallbacks and prohibitions:
   - Prohibit inferred attributes (age, emotion, intentions, relationships).
   - Provide an explicit fallback lexicon (woven basket, pile of fruit, two‑wheeled vehicle, painted metal shutter, signboard, storefront, cart, minivan, pillow) for unverifiable fine classes.

8. Encourage discriminative, short nouns and props:
   - Prefer concrete nouns and visible unique props (e.g., "woven basket", "red bicycle with pannier", "goggles on forehead", "ball near top‑right") over vague adjectives.
   - Penalize generic captions that only list clothing colors or "person walking" without compositional anchors.

9. OCR and visual-text examples in the prompt:
   - Add model examples demonstrating: (a) quoting verified signage correctly, (b) fallback sign descriptions, (c) including a verified micro‑action, (d) using a fine class only with cue‑pair evidence. Use the existing micro‑templates as canonical examples.

10. Deterministic tie‑breakers and cropping policy:
    - When prominence ties, choose larger bbox then leftmost centroid; if subject width >50% image width emit "center".
    - Append "partially cropped at [side]" only when >5% of subject area is outside image.

That will both reduce hallucination and increase alignment with CLIP by favoring short, image‑specific nouns and readable text/props.

High-level goal: make the global captioning prompt enforce the seven‑step numeric verification rules, push for short (10–14 word) discriminative captions, and prioritize verified, scene‑unique tokens (signage, verified micro‑actions, verified fine classes) to raise CLIP image–text alignment.

Concrete, reusable prompt changes (apply to the global prompt text and training/instruction examples):

1) Enforce numeric verification rules explicitly
   - Spell out the exact thresholds used for Count, Contact, Depth, OCR and fine‑class cue‑pairs (e.g., visible_fraction ≥ 0.50, centroid distance ≥ 0.10×width, overlap_ratio thresholds, OCR_conf ≥ 0.70, text_bbox_area ≥ 0.005×image_area). Require the model to output only VERIFIED tokens per these criteria.

2) Front‑load VERIFIED discriminative tokens
   - Instruct: place subject nouns and any VERIFIED discriminative props or quoted text within the first 6–8 words. Provide micro‑templates as exemplars.

3) Strict quoting/OCR policy
   - Require quoting signage verbatim only when OCR_confidence and area/contrast thresholds are met; otherwise produce a compact positional descriptor (e.g., "signboard at upper right"). Prohibit invented characters/brands.

4) Make fine‑class emission conditional on cue‑pairs/classifier confidence
   - Require either classifier_confidence ≥ 0.60 or spatially satisfied cue‑pair within 10% image width before emitting a fine class (bicycle, motorbike, vendor, ladder, performer). Otherwise use the prescribed fallback lexicon.

5) Contact/micro‑action and motion rules
   - Only emit motion verbs or contact micro‑actions when numeric contact/motion evidence is VERIFIED (use overlap ratio + contiguous boundary pixels or classifier_confidence). If borderline, use "near" phrasing. Provide exact micro‑action template and require left/right + part.

6) Depth / foreground tokens only when verified
   - Only include "foreground"/"background" when the numeric depth criteria are met (area ratio + IoU + centroid position or mask unoccluded >60%). Otherwise omit depth tokens.

7) Require spatial relations and counts of salient nearby objects
   - Instruct captioner to list other salient objects and their spatial relation to the subject (left/right/behind/among), but only keep those that are VERIFIED or high‑priority discriminative tokens. Encourage counting only when Count is VERIFIED.

   - Set caption length target to 10–14 words (hard cap 18), remove color/material/lighting/background tokens first when over cap, and keep VERIFIED tokens A–C and part‑relations always. Add a deterministic token removal order and tie‑break rules.

11) Diagnostic logging (for model developers only)
